title: How time is the friend and enemy of learning - 1
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton begins a look at time as a factor affecting learning, arguing that time is both friend and enemy. He shows that knowledge, skills and understanding each need different amounts and kinds of time: short, frequent, spaced bursts for knowledge, longer coached periods for skills, and extended reflection for understanding. He adds that allocated time only helps if students are in good struggle, so under-pitched tasks that leave students treading water waste it. Evidence-gathering also runs at different speeds, quick for knowledge and slowest for understanding, so skills suffer most when schools are crowded. He finishes with curriculum, claiming over-full curricula force coverage over learning and should be written back to front, starting from available time and asking what is the least students can truly learn.
points: Knowledge needs frequent short bursts revisited over a longer period, skills need longer practice with coaching, and understanding needs repeated reflection over months and years.
Time on task only matters if students are in good struggle; tasks pitched too low produce treading water that eats finite learning time.
Skills learning is hit hardest by crowded timetables because both the practice and the evidence about it need slow time.
An over-full curriculum encourages coverage rather than learning, since it leaves no time for good struggle.
Curriculum design should start from the time actually available and ask what is the least students can learn well, like deciding what to leave out of a suitcase.
quotes: Knowledge learning (the repeated exposure to, and the eventual stickiness of, factual information) generally requires frequent, short bursts of time. That’s why Fred Tiramani could happily use register-taking as the time for his students to review, practice and self-test each other on the knowledge they had begun to acquire or were already consolidating.

An indication that skills learning requires more time is that the key activity for teachers in skills learning is coaching. Whichever kind of coaching you think of - sport coaching, life coaching, debate coaching - they all happen over a longer rather than a shorter period of time.

Developing and deepening our understandings is different again. It requires repeated opportunities to reflect over time and see the connection between things and between those things and our lives and personalities.
Being busy but not busy learning is a time-related issue. Being busy can look so good to outsiders and feel good to some under pressure teachers.

Unlike knowledge learning, skills learning really is at the mercy of the time made available to it and the willingness of schools and other organisations (and the people inside those organisations) to commit to making the time available for skills learning and skills assessment. From my own observations, the lack of real good skills learning is not because skills learning isn’t valued by students, parents, teachers, businesses and, to a degree, governments.
What would be helpful is if each curriculum could be written back to front. We need to start first with the time that is available for good learning to happen.
